I encountered several funerals, with few mourners following them, and those who watched regarded them as portents of the gravest kind. Some stared at the processions with frantic eagerness; others shrank away in fear; some cried openly.

After providing immediate relief to the sick, Adrian’s principal concern had been to conceal the plague’s symptoms and advance from the people of London. He understood that fear and gloomy anticipation lent powerful aid to disease, and that despondency and brooding anxiety made the human frame especially liable to infection. Accordingly, no distressing spectacles were visible: most shops remained open, and a certain flow of passers-by was maintained. Yet, though the outward aspect of a stricken city had been averted, London seemed greatly altered to me, who had not seen it since the visitation began. No carriages passed, and tall grass had grown in the streets; the houses looked forlorn, their shutters mostly shut; and the people I encountered wore a pale, frightened stare, wholly unlike the customary businesslike bearing of Londoners. My lone carriage drew attention as it rattled towards the Protectoral Palace, and the fashionable streets approaching it seemed even more dreary and deserted. Adrian’s antechamber was full: it was the appointed hour for audiences. Unwilling to interrupt his work, I waited and observed the petitioners coming and going. They were members of the middle and lower ranks, deprived of their livelihoods by the suspension of trade and of that vigorous pursuit of money in all its forms so characteristic of our country. The anxiety, sometimes terror, of the arrivals contrasted sharply with the resigned, even contented, bearing of those whose audience was over. In their livelier movements and cheerful expressions I could discern my friend’s influence. The clock struck two, and no more were admitted; the disappointed applicants departed sadly or sullenly, while I went into the audience-chamber.

The apparent improvement in Adrian’s health astonished me. He no longer drooped earthward like a spring flower too carefully tended, which grows beyond its strength and bends beneath the very crown of its blossoms. His eyes shone, his face was tranquil, and his entire figure displayed a collected energy far removed from its earlier languor. He was seated at a table among several secretaries, occupied in sorting petitions or recording notes taken in the course of that day’s audiences. Two or three petitioners remained before him. I admired the fairness and patience he showed. To those able to support themselves outside London, he counselled immediate departure, and supplied the means for them to leave.

The next morning, when the Otis family gathered for breakfast, they talked about the ghost at some length. The United States Minister was naturally rather annoyed that his gift had been refused. ‘I have no wish,’ he said, ‘to hurt the ghost personally. And considering how long he has lived in this house, I must say I think throwing pillows at him is very rude.’ This was a perfectly fair remark, though I regret to say that the twins burst into loud laughter. ‘On the other hand,’ he went on, ‘if he really refuses to use the Rising Sun Lubricator, we shall have to take away his chains. No one could possibly sleep with all that noise outside the bedroom doors.’

For the rest of the week, however, nothing disturbed them. The only thing that attracted attention was the bloodstain that kept reappearing on the library floor. This was certainly strange, since Mr. Otis locked the door every night and the windows stayed firmly barred. The stain’s changes of colour also caused plenty of discussion. Some mornings it was a dull, almost Indian red; at other times it was bright scarlet, and then a deep purple. Once, when they came downstairs for family prayers, held according to the simple practices of the Free American Reformed Episcopalian Church, they found it a brilliant emerald green. Naturally, these constantly changing colours greatly amused the family, and every evening they freely placed bets on the subject. Only little Virginia failed to enjoy the joke. For some unexplained reason, the bloodstain always upset her considerably, and on the morning when it was emerald green she almost cried.

The ghost appeared for the second time on Sunday night. Shortly after they had gone to bed, a terrible crash in the hall suddenly startled them. They rushed downstairs and found that a large suit of old armour had come loose from its stand and fallen onto the stone floor. The Canterville ghost sat in a high-backed chair, rubbing his knees, his face showing intense pain. The twins had brought their pea-shooters and immediately fired two pellets at him. Their aim was so accurate that they could only have achieved it through long and careful practice on a handwriting teacher. Meanwhile, the United States Minister pointed his revolver at the ghost and, following Californian manners, ordered him to put up his hands. The ghost jumped up with a wild scream of fury and swept through the family like mist. As he passed, he put out Washington Otis’s candle, leaving them all in complete darkness.

I moved up beside a big, broad fellow with a plump, friendly face, hoping to make myself pleasant and gather a few more scraps of information. But we had barely become acquainted when he began, eagerly and clumsily, to work his way toward that same old story in the time-honoured fashion. It was the one Sir Dinadan had told me when I got into trouble with Sir Sagramor and received his challenge because of it. I excused myself and fell back to the end of the procession, heavyhearted and ready to depart this troubled life, this valley of tears, this short day of interrupted rest, clouds and storms, weary effort and endless defeat. Yet I dreaded the change, remembering how long eternity lasts and how many people who know that story have already gone there.

Early that afternoon we caught up with another procession of pilgrims. Here, though, there was no fun, no joking or laughter, no playfulness, and none of the happy silliness of either young or old. Both young and old were present: grey-haired men and women, strong middle-aged people, young husbands and wives, small boys and girls, and three nursing babies. Even the children never smiled. Every face among those fifty people was downcast, marked by the fixed hopelessness that comes from long suffering and years of knowing despair. They were slaves. Chains connected their shackled ankles and bound wrists to thick leather belts around their waists. Everyone except the children was also joined into a line, six feet apart, by one chain running from collar to collar. They were walking, and had covered three hundred miles in eighteen days, fed on the cheapest scraps and very little even of those. Every night they had slept in their chains, huddled together like pigs. A few miserable rags hung on their bodies, but they could hardly be called dressed. The irons had rubbed the skin off their ankles, leaving open sores full of worms. Their bare feet were torn, and every one of them limped. There had originally been a hundred of these unfortunate people, but about half had been sold along the way. The trader in charge rode a horse and carried a whip with a short handle and a long, heavy lash that split into several knotted ends. Whenever anyone staggered with exhaustion and pain, he slashed their shoulders with it and made them straighten up. He said nothing. The whip made his wishes clear without words.
